questions.q: In the worked example, what is the single isolated difference between Prompt A (control) and Prompt B (challenger)?
options: B adds an order-ID verification step and a refund-escalation rule that A didn't have
B is written in a completely different language
B removes the ability to answer any customer questions
A and B are actually identical prompts
questions.explain: The lesson's example changes exactly one thing in B relative to A: adding a verification step and an escalation rule, so any difference in results can be attributed to that change.

questions.q: Why does the lesson insist on changing only one variable at a time between A and B?
options: Because changing more than one thing is against company policy
Because eval sets can only handle one change per run
Because if multiple things change at once, a result in B's favor doesn't reveal which specific change actually caused the improvement
Because models refuse to process prompts with multiple changes
questions.explain: Changing several things at once makes it impossible to attribute an observed difference to any one specific change — the core reason for isolating a single variable.

questions.q: According to the lesson, when should the comparison metric (pass rate, cost, latency, etc.) be chosen?
options: After seeing the results, to highlight whichever version performed best
Before looking at results, so the choice isn't influenced by a preferred outcome
The metric never needs to be defined explicitly
Only the challenger's team gets to choose the metric
questions.explain: Picking the metric in advance prevents rationalizing a result after the fact by choosing whichever metric happens to favor a preferred version.

questions.q: In the reported result ({prompt_a_pass_rate: 0.738, prompt_b_pass_rate: 0.929, winner: "B", reason: "fewer policy violations"}), why does the specific 'reason' field matter?
options: It doesn't matter — only the pass rates are useful
It is required by JSON syntax and has no functional purpose
It replaces the need to run the eval set at all
It gives a specific, checkable explanation for the win, rather than a vague impression that B 'reads better'
questions.explain: The lesson emphasizes that a trustworthy A/B result reports a specific, checkable reason for the outcome, not just a subjective sense that one version seemed better.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a 2-case difference out of 5 total cases is not a trustworthy basis for shipping a winner?
options: Because such a small sample makes the observed gap likely to be noise rather than a real, reliable signal
Because 5 cases is always too many to run
Because eval sets must contain at least 100 cases to be valid JSON
Because A always wins when the sample is small
questions.explain: The lesson explains that a big-enough sample is needed before shipping a winner, since a tiny difference on very few cases could easily be chance rather than a meaningful improvement.
